summary: MARS: OUTPOST SURVIVAL is a browser-based 2D educational strategy game designed for children aged 7–12. Stepping into the role of Mars Outpost Commander, players lead a crew of four astronauts through a 10-day mission on the Red Planet. Built with plain HTML, CSS, and modular JavaScript requiring no installs, frameworks, or backend servers, the game challenges young learners to balance five core resources—Oxygen, Energy, Food, Water, and Shielding—alongside Crew Health and Research progress.   The project addresses the challenge by transforming real mission planning into interactive daily decisions where every choice carries a visible cost and benefit. Gameplay scenarios are grounded in authoritative NASA sources, including the DONKI space-weather database for solar flare alerts, the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) for space-biology plant research, NASA Mars exploration facts, and Earth–Mars signal travel time calculations. To succeed, players must keep their crew safe through Day 10 and complete at least two of three mission goals: conducting research, growing food in the greenhouse, and sending a report to Earth.   This project is important because it makes space systems engineering accessible to young students, teaching resource interdependence, critical thinking, and scientific honesty through hands-on play.
details:
MARS: OUTPOST SURVIVAL is an interactive, browser-based 2D simulation that places children aged 7–12 in the role of a Mars Outpost Commander. Over a simulated 10-day mission, players must keep a crew of four astronauts alive by managing five interdependent resources: Oxygen, Energy, Food, Water, and Radiation Shielding.

The core gameplay loop centers on daily engineering trade-offs. Each day introduces a scenario grounded in real Mars operational hazards—such as a Coronal Mass Ejection, clogged oxygen scrubbers, or deep-space communication delays. Players are presented with multiple solutions, but every choice has a cost. Boosting life support or repairing a water recycler might consume the electrical energy needed to conduct scientific research or harvest greenhouse crops. To win, players cannot simply hoard one resource; they must survive all 10 days while completing at least two of three mission objectives (Science, Food, and Earth Telemetry).

Benefits & Intended Impact

The primary benefit of the project is translating highly complex aerospace systems engineering into an accessible, low-stakes learning environment. It teaches young students that in space exploration, there are rarely perfect answers—only calculated trade-offs.

Our intended impact is to inspire the Artemis Generation to pursue STEM careers by fostering critical thinking and resource management skills. Furthermore, the game reframes failure: if a player runs out of critical life support, the crew safely evacuates to orbit, and the player is presented with a debriefing screen explaining the science of what went wrong. This encourages iterative learning rather than frustration. Because the application requires zero installations and works completely offline, its impact can reach global classrooms regardless of internet bandwidth.

Tools, Languages & Technologies Used

We engineered the application using a "zero-dependency" philosophy to ensure maximum accessibility and performance.

  • Frontend Languages: Semantic HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla ES6 JavaScript (Modules). We avoided heavy frameworks (like React or Unity) to keep the file size minimal and ensure 100% offline playability.
  • Architecture: A custom-built pure-function rootReducer and a publish/subscribe (pub/sub) state store. This decouples the game math from the DOM rendering, making the resource calculations bug-free and predictable.
  • Development Tools: Visual Studio Code (with the Live Server extension) for rapid local testing and development.
  • Deployment & Hosting: Git and GitHub Pages for seamless, free public hosting and continuous deployment.
  • NASA Data Integrations: NASA's Open APIs (Specifically the DONKI Solar Flare FLR endpoint) accessed via standard JavaScript fetch() promises, supplemented by published research from the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) and Mars Exploration Program telemetry.

Creativity & Innovation

Instead of relying on heavy text or confusing spreadsheets to teach resource balancing, we designed a highly visual "Ghost Bar" UI system. When a player hovers over a decision, GPU-accelerated ghost bars render directly over their outpost meters, showing exactly how much of a resource will be gained or lost before they commit to the action. This creatively turns complex subtraction and addition into intuitive visual spatial reasoning for young minds.

Additionally, we utilized a Reactive Living SVG Scene. Instead of static images, the 2D Mars outpost dynamically changes based on the game's mathematical state. If a dust storm rolls in, the sky turns a hazy orange; if energy levels drop below critical, the habitat windows dim; and if the greenhouse objective is met, the hydroponic crops visibly glow.

Factors Our Team Considered

  • Scientific Honesty & Transparency: We wanted to ensure kids knew the difference between real science and a game mechanic. We built a dedicated "Science & Data" screen that explicitly separates Real NASA Data, Derived Orbital Math, Fictional Story Events, and Game Assumptions.
  • Accessibility (a11y): We ensured the game could be played by everyone. Every color-coded status (like green for OK or red for Empty) is paired with a distinct emoji icon and text label for colorblind users. The entire UI supports keyboard-only navigation with visible focus rings, and ARIA live regions announce critical alerts to screen readers.
  • Network Resilience: Hackathons and classrooms often suffer from spotty Wi-Fi. We designed the live NASA DONKI space-weather API fetch with a graceful fallback. If the network drops or the API rate-limits, the game instantly switches to a curated NASA archive record, guaranteeing the presentation and gameplay never break.
